title: Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41)
hook: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner becomes governor

segments.voice: Yesterday, prison: a false charge, a cell, and a butler who forgot. Your line was the lord was with joseph. Where did you do right when no one saw? Day three hundred sixty-three.

Two years later, Pharaoh has a nightmare. He's standing by the Nile, and seven cows come up out of the river, sleek and fat, and graze in the reeds. Then seven more come up behind them, thin, ugly, all bone. And the thin cows eat the fat ones, and look no better afterward. He wakes, falls back asleep, and dreams again: seven full ears of grain on one stalk, swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones. Every wise man in Egypt is summoned. Nobody can explain it. And then the butler, the one who forgot, suddenly remembers: there was a young Hebrew in prison who read dreams. Joseph is pulled out of the dungeon, shaved, given clean clothes, and stood in front of the king.
screen: `SEVEN FAT COWS, SEVEN THIN.` → `NOBODY CAN EXPLAIN IT.` → `THE BUTLER REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Pharaoh says he hears Joseph can read dreams. Joseph's first words turn that around: it isn't in him, he says; God will give Pharaoh his answer. Then the meaning. Seven years of plenty are coming to Egypt, and after them seven years of famine so heavy the good years will be forgotten. The dream came twice, Joseph says, because the thing is settled. Then he does something nobody asked him to do. He doesn't stop at the warning. He gives a plan. Find a wise man. Set overseers over the land. Take a fifth of the harvest in each good year and store it in the cities, so that when the lean years come, the country doesn't die. Pharaoh looks around his court and says, in effect, where would we find another man with the spirit of God in him? He puts his ring on Joseph's hand, dresses him in fine linen, hangs a gold chain around his neck, and makes him governor of all Egypt. Joseph is thirty. He was seventeen when his brothers sold him. Then it plays out exactly. Seven fat years, grain piled up like the sand of the sea. Then the famine, in every land. The people cry to Pharaoh for bread, and he answers in three words: "Go to Joseph." Catholics have borrowed that line for a different Joseph. Saint Joseph, the husband of Mary, also listened to dreams and also took his family down to Egypt, and in 1870 Pope Pius the Ninth named him patron of the whole Church. In Latin, Ite ad Ioseph, go to Joseph, still appears in prayers and on altars to Saint Joseph.
screen: `NOT IN ME: GOD WILL ANSWER.` · `SEVEN YEARS FULL, SEVEN YEARS LEAN.` · `STORE A FIFTH IN THE GOOD YEARS.` · `GO TO JOSEPH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put something by for a lean time. Settle, and breathe. Think about the season you're in. If it's a full one, what could you store from it? A little money. A meal in the freezer. A thank-you note you could reread on a hard day. A friendship you could tend now, before you need it. If it's a lean season already, think back to a full one and notice what it left you. Choose one small thing to put by today. If you pray, you can offer the full years and the lean ones to God. If you don't, just sit with the thought of both. The bell holds the time.
Pharaoh's dreams. Seven fat cows and seven thin ones: a warning of plenty, then famine, that Joseph reads and turns into a plan. Today's word.
Your line: plan for the lean years. Today, set one thing aside, money or food or kindness, for a day that will need it. Day three hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Many Catholics turn to Saint Joseph as patron of the universal Church, of workers and of families in need, and the old phrase Ite ad Ioseph, go to Joseph, appears in devotions to him, especially in March, the month traditionally given to Saint Joseph.

that's Joseph's own explanation of the doubled dream.

fork.setup: you're Joseph, just out of prison. you've told Pharaoh what the dreams mean: seven full years, then seven lean. what do you say next?
options: offer a plan: store a fifth of each good harvest.
ask to be set free and sent home.
fork.reveal: unasked, he gives a plan: overseers, and a fifth of the harvest stored in the cities. Pharaoh makes him governor on the spot.

original.note: Hebrew for the Egyptian title per-aa, great house: first the palace, later the king who lived there.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange dream about cows.
what it means: a warning of plenty and famine, read rightly and turned into a plan to store grain in the good years.
what a scholar hears: Joseph's new Egyptian name in 41:45 is hard to decode; the Latin Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims render it savior of the world.

sources.ref: Quemadmodum Deus (decree naming Saint Joseph patron of the universal Church, 1870)

notes: Joseph's age: seventeen at Genesis 37:2, thirty at 41:46. Confirm.
Pharaoh's words at 41:38 paraphrased ('another man with the spirit of God in him').
Genesis 41:45: Zaphenath-paneah (Hebrew); the Vulgate gives 'Salvatorem mundi' and the Douay-Rheims 'The saviour of the world'. Confirm the DR wording before the trapdoor goes out.
Pius IX declared Saint Joseph patron of the universal Church on December 8, 1870 (decree Quemadmodum Deus). Confirm.
'Ite ad Ioseph' applied to Saint Joseph in devotion and on altars: stated generally; confirm it is fair.
Pharaoh from Egyptian per-aa, 'great house': standard etymology; confirm.
Some readers also hear an echo of Mary at Cana (John 2:5) in the full verse ('do all that he shall say to you'); left out to keep one idea.
